segments.text: Catherine, welcome to the Health Committee. It's very good to have you here.
We have you here for 10 minutes.
You may use that time as you wish. If you want to leave us any time for
questions, you may. I'll leave that time with you and hand it to you
now. Welcome.
Thank you.
Can I just remind the committee, I'm actually completely deaf in my left ear, so if
you could raise your voices if you do have any
questions to ask of me. I may not hear them.
Absolutely. Thank you.
Okay, so I can go?
You can go, yes.
Good morning, Mr. Chair and members of the Health Select Committee.
Thank you for the opportunity to appear before you and for considering my written
submission and supporting fiscal assessment.
You already have the clinical evidence, international comparison,
patient experiences, and financial analysis before
you. I do not want to use my limited time repeating them.
I want to tell you what those pages mean in real life, and why I
believe this committee now has an opportunity to create a turning point.
I came before you with the resounding voices of
17,096 New Zealanders who signed my
petition.
I'm supported here with Annette Wickepa, one of the courageous patient
advocates who fought the government of the time nearly 20 years ago
for access to Herceptin for HER2 positive breast cancer, and Annette
deserves a place at the table.
Annette and other women stood before decision-makers like you, asking New
Zealand to fund the recognized full treatment pathway for their breast cancer.
Nearly two decades later, I'm here doing the same thing for triple-negative breast
cancer.
Different medicine, different subtype, but the same fundamental
issue.
New Zealand continues to fund partial breast cancer
pathways while leaving patients and families to fight for the medicine that may
complete their treatment.
I was diagnosed with high-risk triple-negative breast cancer following a routine
screening mammogram. Up until that point, I was extremely
well. Triple-negative breast cancer, as you know, is aggressive.
It's fast-moving and has fewer targeted treatment options.
For eligible patients, timing is treatment.
The internationally recognized KEYNOTE-522 regimen
provides Keytruda with chemotherapy before surgery and
continues Keytruda after surgery while treatment is still being delivered with
curative intent.
New Zealand funds diagnosis, it funds chemotherapy, it
funds surgery, it funds radiotherapy.
But it does not fund Keytruda for eligible early-stage triple-negative breast
cancer patients, even though it is the medicine that completes the
internationally recognized regime.
That is not a complete treatment pathway.
It is a partial pathway.
Politicians across the house yesterday talked about how much money that
they have provided to Pharmac, and that is great.
That is a great start, but it is only a start.
And full treatment is ... Sorry, I need to
put my glasses on.
Can't read my own writing.
It's all right. Take your time.
We all have that problem.
Politicians across the house yesterday talked about what has been provided
to Pharmac, and that is good, but you cannot celebrate the gaping hole.
Full treatment is not a brand-new hospital without the medicine.
Partial cancer pathways are cruel.
Scans identify an aggressive cancer but deny many patients access
to the treatment that may reduce their risk of recurrence.
We celebrate early diagnosis but fail to provide early access to the
treatment supported by that diagnosis.
This leaves families facing a long, painful decline to stage four
metastatic or financial hardship.
One of the earliest questions I was asked after diagnosis was whether I had private
health insurance.
Because I did, I entered the private pathway, and I was offered
KEYNOTE-522.
I'm really unclear of the real benefit, only that the public system
was saved from all the costs through my private insurance for chemo,
surgery, and obviously radiotherapy.
At no stage was I offered the option of receiving my
funded chemotherapy publicly while privately paying for
Keytruda, which would've helped me immensely.
My private insurance benefit was exhausted, and I incurred approximately
$300,000 in additional intravenous treatment and
administration costs. As I explained to Huhana
yesterday, a saline bag, which was required for me for
hydration, which is required for many patients, cost me
$500 to have that saline bag given to me and
infused.
Those costs were not caused by the medicine alone.
They were caused by a fragmented pathway, and I stand before you today
in remission, and I'm profoundly grateful to be alive.
But staying alive came at an extraordinary cost.
We had to fund $130,000 for my treatment, for which
strangers, family, and friends funded $73,000, and I
still owe approximately $50,000.
However, that is not the biggest issue.
The uncertainty surrounding my treatment also meant I was forced to
list my home, get out of bed while I was going through chemo, and
forced to sell a business in a tough economic environment, as
we could not raise money against our assets.
We lost our business at a loss of $700,000.
I sit in front of you having lost $750,000, and the
reality is, is that I'm now in discussions with my bank at losing my home.
That business represented decades and decades of my hard work,
my family's hard work, sacrifice, and investment.
My story is the story of many, many New
Zealanders. Cancer threatened my life and theirs,
but the funding pathway fundamentally altered the financial future
our families had spent a lifetime building.
We've paid our taxes all through our working life.
I paid for private health insurance. I built businesses.
I employed people. I've contributed to New Zealand.
My children are service-related children in the service.
Yet I stand before you approximately 750,000 poorer
because I developed an aggressive cancer and wanted the treatment recognized
internationally, and I wanted to stay alive.
I feel that this government and consecutive government have
failed me and thousands of others.
I'm alive, laden with the guilt of our family financial hardship,
but I'm also laden with the guilt that I am alive.
You see, Amber Rose, who was diagnosed not long after me, is now
deceased. Amber Rose reached out to me, and like me, she
was diagnosed with stage three triple negative breast cancer.
A 45-year-old solo mother of four children, three
of them under 16. She went through the public system, and because she was a
solo mom, she was never offered Keynote 522.
When her cancer returned, which was less than six months later,
it had spread through her bones, liver, lungs, and lymphatic.
She said, "Catherine, the grief is overwhelming. I want to live.
My children need me, and I am so scared."
Amber died on the 13th of May 2026,
14 months from diagnosis. That is how aggressive triple
negative breast cancer is. I remind the committee, I'm sitting here.
I had the same stage, the same type, and the same
length that she had. She will not see her children grow up.
I cannot tell you that Keytruda would've saved her. I am not a doctor.
No one can. But I can tell you she was never given the same
opportunity I received while her disease was still being treated with
curative intent. She deserved the opportunity to live, and that
opportunity could not be recovered later. This is inequity.
Two women can have the same aggressive disease at the same stage.
One received the internationally recognized treatment because she has
insurance, assets, savings, or a community to fundraise.
The other may not even be told that treatment exists.
In my written submission, I provided you another lady, Jackie Toy, who
was never advised of Keytruda, and these are stories that have been told across
the nation to me every day.
The biology of our cancer is still the same.
It is still aggressive. The difference is our financial
capacity and the pathway through which they enter or we enter
the system.
Clinical needs to be determined by treatment, not
financial means. I'm asking the committee to look beyond the
price of one medicine. I know I'm only allowed to talk about Keytruda, but
I'm asking you to look beyond the price of one medicine.
This government has repeatedly spoken about getting more impact from every dollar
spent, ensuring every dollar count, and delivering better value for money.
This is precisely why Keytruda must be assessed through a whole of government lens.
Funding earlier at early stage while treatment is intended to cure
may represent substantially better value than repeatedly paying after
cancer has progressed. Progression creates cost
across hospital oncology, imaging, emergency care,
hospital mental health, welfare, employment, productivity,
tax revenue, caregivers, hospice, and financial family
security. And that is why I have written to MPs across the
whole House, across all portfolios, and I do not apologize for
doing so.
We regularly calculate the cost of funding medicine.
We rarely calculate the full cost of not funding them.
A recent public policy commentary by Cathy Spencer, a former senior
leader across the Ministry of Health, ACC, and Treasury, highlighted a
profound inconsistency in how New Zealand values lives.
Treasury currently places a value of approximately
16.6 million on preventing one road death,
yet values one year of healthy life at only
36,670 for health investment analysis.
That raises a fundamental question.
Why is a life valued so differently depending on whether the risk arises on a
road or through cancer?
If government is serious about achieving more impact from every dollar
spent, then the value of extending and protecting life must be
assessed consistently across the public sector.
The value of life should inform the medicine budget, and the size of the medicine
budget should not determine how little a life is worth.
This is not a request for you to abandon fiscal discipline.
It is a request to apply fiscal discipline properly by
investing where treatment can deliver the greatest clinical and economic
return. More impact from every health dollar should mean
investing before decline, not merely paying to manage
decline after the opportunity for cure has been lost.
The Health Select Committee is not powerless in this.
You can scrutinize the performance and priorities of health agencies.
You can require information. You can question officials,
and you can examine where the current funding settings reflect clinical
evidence, equity, and value of public money.
You can recommend further inquiry and action, and I respectfully ask
you to use those powers. I ask the committee to recommend
urgent public funding of Keytruda for
eligible high-risk early-stage triple negative breast cancer.
Women have given so much to society and deserve a fighting chance to
live. I've given this over 1,200 of unpaid hours
during a time I've been fighting for my life.
I ask you to recommend a review of the restrictive advanced stage
criteria and a patient-centered approach where funding allows clinical
need where a person cannot tolerate the funded medicine.
Can I ask you to recognize the wider
The wider warning carried by this petition.
I might be here for Keytruda. 20 years ago, Annette was here for
others for Herceptin. Tomorrow, another patient will be here for another
medicine unless New Zealand develops a sustainable long-term health and
medicine strategy. Bouncing me and other patients around
between MPs and ministers, or placing this directly at one minister's
door is not the way that we should be doing
things. We cannot keep addressing access one patient, one
petition, one desperate crowdfunding campaign at a time.
Health needs a bipartisan approach.
Without health, we have nothing. New Zealanders and the Pacific nations that
we claim to support need full cancer pathways.
On behalf of the 17,096 New Zealanders who signed this petition,
we're asking for temanako, for hope.
We hope that early diagnosis will be matched by early treatment.
We hope that another mother will see her children grow up.
I hope that the family will not lose everything they've spent a lifetime building.
Let Annette's legacy and my commitment and the voices of 17,000 New
Zealanders become a turning point.
A turning point where New Zealand recognizes that saving lives and saving public
money are not competing objectives.
In this case, they are aligned. Again, I
remind you, this has not been about me.
It has always been about the next person who hears the words, "You have early-stage
triple negative cancer."
My dream is that one day the next words will be, "Don't worry.
In New Zealand, you'll receive the best treatment in the world."
I want to tell you one last thing. My fear for
me personally is that I've fought this war, and I will continue to fight it
till the end, and you will continue to hear from me.
But I may have another war that may return if my cancer returns, and that
scares me, that I'm fighting this, and I'm still not saving
myself. So thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the
committee. I welcome your openness and questions, and I
welcome your continued conversation with me beyond this meeting.
Thank you, Ms. Cook. Thank you. Unfortunately, we're over time
by a number of minutes, but I want to say-
Are you able to speak up, Stan?
... absolute pleasure to have you here, Ms. Cook.
I thank you for your very impassioned submission,
and all of the hard work and
recognizing, acknowledging the struggles,
personally and financially, that you have and your family has faced through
this process. Thank you for all of your work in this space.
Cheers.
Thank you. We won't be having questions, unfortunately.
We're a fair few minutes over time.
If you don't have any questions, I have some more things to talk about.
Oh, we are over time.
We're out of time?
We're out of time. Yes.
Oh, okay. All right. Well, you're welcome to come and give me those questions at
another time, but-
Yes
... I'm sorry if I did go over time, and I hope that-
No, no
... I've been able to at least tell you that I'm just
a normal human, passionate Kiwi girl.
And Nicola Willis said yesterday brave and extraordinary.
Other people call me a hero. I'm not.
I didn't ask to get cancer, and I know that none of you
want to be doing the jobs that you're doing, and I do appreciate the gravity of the
work that you do. But we have to change, and I'm asking all of
you across government to really look at this as a
whole of government issue. And please don't tell me how much you've
put in the pot. The pot is empty
and people need the bridge gaped.
Thank you, Catherine.
All right. Thank you so much for your time.
Thanks, Annette.
Yeah.
It's heavy, but thank you.
Where do you think?
All right. We'll move back to
private session.

Include anything that might incriminate or cast

Tēnā koutou katoa. Thank you so much for the opportunity to speak today.
My name is Casey Spirin. I'm the general manager of Know Your Stuff NZ
Charitable Trust. We are a peer-led harm reduction nonprofit,
and our goal is to reduce and prevent the harms caused in drugs in New Zealand by
providing evidence and advice, including carrying out drug checking and
advocating for an evidence-based harm reduction approach to drug policy, which is
why we're here today.
For over 12 years now, we've provided non-judgmental harm reduction services and
education. Last year, our team of 500 volunteers hosted
189 events ranging from small town drug checking clinics
to large festivals, and we checked drug samples for over 5,000 clients.
I'd like to begin by acknowledging Kahurangi Carter for her work in getting this
bill before the House, and the Drug Foundation and everyone else who's advocated
for this for decades.
I'd also like to acknowledge the courage and vulnerability of the previous
submitters who've shared deeply personal stories of overdose and loss.
These stories are really important.
They move this conversation away from this abstract
subject of a drug user and remind us that we're really talking
about our children, and our siblings, and our parents, and our friends.
There is no typical drug user in Aotearoa.
And I'd encourage everyone listening to consider that there are people in your
communities
and close circles who use illicit drugs, whether or not you're aware of it.
Taking our written submission as read, we strongly support this bill.
We urge the committee to recommend that it proceed as written,
including providing the broad protection for people at the scene
and a wide range of harm incidents, including acute
psychological distress and not just physical overdose, and protection for
the low-level offenses listed.
This bill is simple and practical and evidence-based, and it
gives people clarity and certainty at the exact moment that they need it
when someone's life is at risk, and they're deciding whether or not to pick up the
phone.
We also consider this bill to be a matter of equity and
clarity. I know that the Misuse of Drugs Act amendment in 2019
directs police to apply discretion for personal possession and use, and to consider
whether a health-based approach is in the public interest.
In practice, we know that this discretion is not evenly applied across different
communities, and this bill helps to correct that inequity.
It provides consistent, simple, understandable protection for
people who are disproportionately overpoliced for low-level drug
offenses, rather than leaving the safety dependent on discretion
where they live or who responds to the call.
And it aligns with the direction that we've already set for taking a
health-first approach to personal drug use.
One thing that we would really like to presence in this is that this bill could be
a small level of protection that we desperately
need in terms of the changing drug supply and
market. At the current overdose rates that we're seeing right
now, the Drug Foundation estimates that this law would save something between 18
and 29 lives per year. That's enough reason to pass it.
We are already losing people. But there's a reason to act now rather
than later. Over a dozen other OECD countries, including
Canada and all US states, already have laws of this kind.
We need to take this opportunity while our overdose rates are comparatively
low to many of these places overseas.
Last year, the Ministerial Advisory Group on Organized Crime reported that drug
seizures no longer have any discernible impact on drug supply or
consumption. The availability of illicit substances is rapidly
increasing overseas and here.
And novel psychoactive substances are being developed more quickly
than we can identify and legislate for them.
In our work in drug checking, we know that potent and high-risk substances can show
up in any of the drug types that are taken in New Zealand at any
point. This is not an issue that we are going to be able
to arrest our way out of. We need to be able to respond to this
change in the market because currently we're not protected from a
toxic and fast-changing drug supply.
So passing this bill now, we have the opportunity to have these
conversations to think carefully about implementation as a way
that we can start to build these systems to protect people for if and
when that changes, because I know certainly a lot of us that work in harm reduction
are waiting for the when, not the if,
rather than having to look at this in an escalating crisis under
urgency.
The metaphor used in that report was that our current approach is akin to
rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic.
I would consider this bill to be a lifeboat.
It's a small one. It's not going to change everything, but it will save
lives and will buy us time in a crisis.
If it passes, obviously our work isn't finished.
Our clients, especially our younger clients, are very afraid of the
authorities. Frankly, they're afraid to come to
us, and we do operate in a very clear legal framework.
So it's really vital that this is followed by community
education and outreach, that people know that these protections exist and can trust
them,
and is followed up by
increasing access to addiction and mental health support, more drug
checking, more access to naloxone, particularly nasal spray
naloxone, and community training in overdose recognition and
response.
This bill isn't going to stop people from using drugs. That's not the point of it.
But what it does make sure is that when something goes wrong,
people don't hesitate to make a phone call that could save a life.
People aren't trying to make complex decisions in a moment of crisis.
And for that, we do urge the committee to recommend that it proceed.
Thank you. I'm very happy to take any questions.
Excellent. Any members? Jenny Marcroft.
Oh, thank you very much for your submission.
In your submission, you have
said that you have evidence that fear of the law pushes
people to do the wrong thing. Could you please provide that evidence to the
committee?
I believe that this evidence has been probably brought up in many
other submissions as well. Morally, we
would say that calling an ambulance in the case of an overdose,
in the case of a crisis, is the right thing to do.
We want to encourage people to do the right thing.
Because this fear of prosecution, because this fear of ending up in the criminal
justice system while you're trying to help someone does exist.
We know that the Drug Foundation has done
surveys on this showing that something about 40% of people would be
hesitating to call.
To me, that's just clear there.
So just for clarification, thank you, Mr. Chair, for supplementary.
Yes.

New Zealand. But it seemed quite defeatist in the sense that we can't

directing police resources to dealing with these large-scale supply
issues rather than personal use and crisis.
To speak from personal experience as someone from British Columbia,

when these things get going, it moves quickly, and we have

and many people close to me as well.

to you now. Thank you.
Perfect. Cool. Mōrena koutou. So I'm Sam Lasham, one of the
founders and the national coordinator for Students for Sensible Drug Policy
Aotearoa. We're a group of students and young people who advocate for our vision
of an Aotearoa free from drug harm.
I'm also a harm reduction researcher as well.
So 36 lives lost. That's the estimated number of people we've
lost to overdose in the 12 weeks since you sat down for the first
reading of this bill. It hasn't been that long, and that is a
considerable loss to this country.
This bill could have led to around maybe even five or six of these people still
being here based on overseas evidence.
It's not often that we get to discuss a bill that would save lives of almost no
cost to the taxpayer, so thank you for the opportunity to talk about saving lives
with you today.
You'll obviously have seen our written submission, so I won't rehash all the
points, but I'll just give you a summary, discuss some misunderstandings, and leave
some time for questions. So drugs harm is a severe
issue in New Zealand. As you will have heard by now from that Drug Foundation
report, we lose about three people to overdose a week.
And
that Drug Foundation survey that Casey just mentioned found that about
40% of respondents would be fearful to call for help for someone experiencing drug
harm. Beyond that,
also we see this as people that work in the space, we routinely have
this conversation. Through my own work, literally within the
last few weeks, I have talked to people who have had to call an ambulance in these
sorts of situations and have been scared.
It's not just the fear of prosecution, but also a fear of
mistreatment, a fear that even if they do call the ambulance, they might not get
taken seriously or get the adequate help that they need as well because
of the stigma that's so prevalent in our society and because of a history of people
who use drugs being mistreated by health and justice sectors.
Stigma is not a rational being, and even if statistically people are unlikely to
be arrested when calling in an overdose, they need legal certainty to be
certain of that fact. Evidence from overseas shows that such
legislation could result in around a 15% reduction in overdose
deaths, and that reductions may be greater for more heavily marginalized groups as
well.
So our review of the literature around such legislation identified that these
policies overseas have been limited by a lack of public awareness,
and measures to increase that awareness could really improve the effectiveness of
this bill. So I think that's something that really should be considered.
Additionally, I believe the New Zealand Law Society has also raised along these
lines that there's some difficulty determining when these illegal exemptions would
apply, and we believe that it'd be in the interest of everyone if this bill simply
covered all instances of harm, just to make things
simpler. Drug use doesn't occur in a vacuum, and currently as
written, it appears the bill would not give protection to people who may be
hesitant to call for help over other emergencies that may occur in the vicinity
of drug use but may not be drug-related.
A good example of this might be like an alcohol overdose at a party where drugs are
being used.
Expanding this would reduce confusion around the bill and also increase its
potential benefits as well. So just to cover a
couple of points about what we believe might have been some misinterpretations
we've heard about people as the discussion of this bill has
progressed over the last few months.
There appears to be some misunderstandings around who might be protected
under this legislation and whether it would protect people who sell drugs from
prosecution. I think some of that comes from confusion around this idea of
social supply. And social supply is a very common
activity that is distinct from commercial sale.
It is essentially the sharing of drugs between friends, just like you might
buy a box of beers and give one to a friend when they visit.
Just as we don't expect you to have a liquor license to give a beer to your
friend, this bill makes a similar separation between people who share drugs with
their friends and those who are selling drugs for profit.
The former would not be
prosecuted, and the latter still would
be.
So some of the other big objections to this bill appear to be from a view that
criminalizing people who use drugs, and even people suffering from an overdose,
will reduce drug use and overdose deaths.
Unfortunately, it's not that simple, and if it was, then we wouldn't be here
today as the last 50 years of criminalization of people who use drugs would have
solved this issue. Alas, it has not, and in fact, drug
use continues to increase despite our criminalization approach.
Contrary to public perception, there is not a strong relationship between
the criminalization of people who use drugs and the rate of drug use and drug
harm that occurs in a country.
This is clear from numerous jurisdictions recently decriminalizing drug
possession overseas, and either seeing no change in drug use or
harm or seeing a small reduction in such measures.
I'll gladly forward some papers showing that to anyone here who is
interested in that.
Also, I know I have heard some people posit this bill should consider
compulsory treatment instead of a criminal approach.
Anything such as this that could be seen as punishment will increase hesitancy
to call for help and will lead to a greater number of overdose
deaths. So SSDP strongly recommends against this.
Such measures are also considerably wasteful, particularly as the majority of
people who use drugs or who are bystanders to an overdose may not
experience addiction, and forcing treatment on those who do not want it
is typically ineffective.
So that's the majority of my points, but yeah, I've tried to leave a reasonable
amount of time to give you guys a chance to ask some questions.
So thank you.
